mainEntity.name: How do underwriters calculate self-employed income for a mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Underwriters start with the net income on your federal tax returns — not your gross revenue and not your bank deposits — then run a cash flow analysis using a worksheet like Fannie Mae Form 1084 or Freddie Mac Form 91. They add back paper deductions that didn't actually cost you cash, such as depreciation, depletion, amortization, casualty losses, and business use of home. Then they typically average the result over two years to get a qualifying monthly income.

mainEntity.name: What deductions get added back to self-employed income?

acceptedAnswer.text: For Schedule C filers, the standard add-backs are depreciation, depletion, amortization, casualty losses, and the business-use-of-home deduction. These are deductions that reduce taxable income but don't reduce the cash your business actually generated. What does NOT get added back: real cash expenses like vehicle costs, supplies, contract labor, meals, and travel. If you wrote it off and it was a real expense, it lowers your qualifying income.

mainEntity.name: Do I need two years of self-employment to get a mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually, but not always. Fannie Mae generally wants a two-year history of self-employment. There is an exception: with at least twelve full months of self-employment income on your most recent federal tax return, you may still qualify if you previously earned similar or greater income in the same field before going out on your own. Less than twelve months on a tax return is very difficult on conventional financing — that's usually a bank statement or non-QM conversation.

mainEntity.name: What happens if my self-employment income went down from one year to the next?

acceptedAnswer.text: Declining income changes the math. When income is stable or rising, underwriters average the two years. When the most recent year is lower, they generally can't use the higher average — the analysis leans on the lower, more recent figure, and the underwriter has to be satisfied the decline has stabilized. A one-time dip with a documented reason is workable. A steady downtrend is a harder conversation, and pretending it isn't there doesn't help you.

mainEntity.name: What if my tax returns don't show enough income to qualify?

acceptedAnswer.text: You have two real options. Option one is planning ahead: work with your CPA in the tax year before you buy so the returns show the income you actually earn — that trade costs some tax but buys qualifying power. Option two is a loan built for this exact situation: a bank statement loan qualifies you on business deposits instead of net tax income, and other non-QM programs qualify on assets or property cash flow. Aggressive write-offs don't end your homebuying plans — they just change which loan fits.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between a DSCR loan and a conventional investment property loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: The core difference is what the loan qualifies on. A conventional investment property loan qualifies on your personal income and debt-to-income ratio — you provide tax returns, W-2s or pay stubs, and the lender measures whether your income covers all your debt. A DSCR loan qualifies on the property's rent instead, using the Debt Service Coverage Ratio: monthly rent divided by the property's monthly principal, interest, taxes, and insurance. DSCR loans are made for a business purpose, so they sit outside the consumer ability-to-repay rule and don't require personal income verification. Conventional loans generally price lower; DSCR loans qualify more investors and close without touching your tax returns.

mainEntity.name: Is a DSCR loan or a conventional loan cheaper for a Texas rental?

acceptedAnswer.text: Conventional investment-property financing almost always carries a lower rate than a comparable DSCR loan, because it's a fully documented loan sold to Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac. A DSCR loan trades some rate for the convenience of qualifying on rent instead of personal income. The right question isn't which rate is lower in a vacuum — it's whether you can qualify conventionally at all, and what the lower-rate conventional loan costs you in tax returns, DTI room, and the cap on how many properties you can finance. For a W-2 investor buying their first or second rental, conventional usually wins on cost. For a self-employed or portfolio investor, DSCR often wins on access.

mainEntity.name: How many investment properties can I finance with conventional vs DSCR loans?

acceptedAnswer.text: Fannie Mae caps a borrower at 10 financed 1-4 unit properties when the new loan is for a second home or investment property, and reserve requirements increase as your property count rises. Once you hit that conventional ceiling — or once your debt-to-income ratio from existing mortgages blocks the next deal — DSCR loans have no such national cap, because they qualify each property on its own rent rather than stacking against your personal DTI. That's the practical reason most Texas investors who scale past a handful of doors end up on DSCR financing for the later purchases.

mainEntity.name: Do DSCR loans require tax returns in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. A DSCR loan qualifies on the property's rent and your credit, reserves, and down payment — not your personal income — so there are no tax returns, W-2s, or pay stubs in the file. This is why DSCR is the standard answer for self-employed investors, 1099 earners, and anyone whose tax returns show strong write-offs that crush their qualifying income on a conventional loan. A conventional investment property loan, by contrast, requires the full personal income documentation package.

Portfolio jumbo investors price off their own balance sheet and ignore LLPAs entirely.

mainEntity.name: What's the difference between QM jumbo and non-QM jumbo?

Non-QM jumbo uses alternative income documentation: bank statements (12-24 months), 1099-only, P&L statements, or asset depletion. Same loan amounts, different qualifying path. Non-QM is built for self-employed, business owners, and asset-heavy buyers whose tax returns understate their true cash flow.

mainEntity.name: What's the DTI cap on a jumbo loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most jumbo programs cap debt-to-income at 43%, though portfolio lenders flex to 45-50% with strong compensating factors (large reserves, big down payment, significant non-retirement assets). Asset depletion files can effectively ignore DTI by counting liquid assets as imputed income.

mainEntity.name: What does non-QM mean on a mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Non-QM means a loan doesn't meet the CFPB's Qualified Mortgage standard under 12 CFR 1026.43(e) — the rule that caps debt-to-income ratios and requires income to be verified using specific, standardized methods. It does not mean bad credit or high risk by default. It means the lender is documenting your income a different way, often because you're self-employed, an investor, or your money doesn't show up as a W-2. The lender still has to make a good-faith determination that you can repay the loan — that ability-to-repay requirement applies whether or not the loan is a QM.

mainEntity.name: Is a non-QM loan bad or risky?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not inherently. Non-QM is a documentation category, not a credit-quality label. I've closed non-QM loans for physicians, business owners with seven-figure net worth, and investors with dozens of properties — all denied by their bank not because they couldn't afford the home, but because their income doesn't fit a W-2 box. Pricing on non-QM loans tends to run higher than conventional because these loans carry more manual underwriting and typically aren't sold to Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac, not because the borrower is a worse credit risk.

mainEntity.name: Why did my bank say I don't qualify even though I make good money?

acceptedAnswer.text: Almost always it's how your income is calculated, not how much you actually make. Fannie Mae's underwriting guidelines require lenders to qualify self-employed borrowers off net income from tax returns — after every deduction and write-off — averaged over two years. A business owner who nets $40,000 on paper while running $250,000 through the business can look unqualified to a conventional underwriter even though the bank statements tell a completely different story.

mainEntity.name: What are the main types of non-QM loans in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: The core categories are bank statement loans (income based on deposits instead of tax returns), DSCR loans (investment properties qualified on the property's rental income instead of your personal debt-to-income), asset depletion loans (assets converted into a monthly income figure), 1099 and ITIN programs for non-traditional workers and non-citizen borrowers, and jumbo non-QM for high-net-worth buyers whose full financial picture doesn't fit standard boxes. Each has its own qualifying method — none of them are one-size-fits-all.

mainEntity.name: Do DSCR loans qualify off my personal income?

acceptedAnswer.text: No — that's the whole point of a DSCR loan. Conventional investment-property loans still qualify you off your personal debt-to-income ratio, with the rental income added in under Fannie Mae's rental-income guidelines. A DSCR loan flips that: the property's own rental income relative to its debt payment is what qualifies the loan, largely independent of your personal W-2 or tax-return income. That's why an investor with ten properties and complicated tax returns can often qualify for the eleventh through DSCR when a conventional loan would drown in the math.

mainEntity.name: What does non-QM mean on a mortgage?

mainEntity.name: When does it make sense to refinance a mortgage in 2026?

acceptedAnswer.text: Refinance when your break-even point — the number of months it takes for monthly savings to cover the closing costs — is shorter than the time you'll stay in the home. The old rule of thumb was a 1% rate drop, but that rule ignores closing costs and how long you actually plan to keep the loan. In 2026, most Austin homeowners need to drop their rate by 0.5% to 0.75% and stay in the home for at least 3 years for a refinance to pay off. If you're planning to sell within 18 months, refinancing almost never makes sense.

mainEntity.name: How do I calculate the break-even point on a refinance?

acceptedAnswer.text: Divide your total closing costs by your monthly payment savings. If closing costs are $6,000 and you save $200 per month, the break-even is 30 months — you need to keep the loan at least 30 months to recover the cost. If you plan to stay 5 years, a 30-month break-even is a good deal. If you might move in 2 years, it's a loss. The math is that simple. Don't let anyone sell you on a refinance without running this number first.

mainEntity.name: What are typical closing costs on a refinance in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: Refinance closing costs in Texas typically run 2% to 4% of the loan amount. On a $400,000 loan, expect $8,000 to $16,000 in total costs, including lender fees, title insurance, appraisal, and recording. Texas has some unique rules — a cash-out refinance here is treated under Texas A6 law, which caps total fees at 2% of the loan amount and adds specific disclosure requirements. A rate-and-term refinance doesn't fall under A6 and has more standard pricing.

mainEntity.name: Should I do a cash-out refinance to pay off credit card debt?

acceptedAnswer.text: Only if you're confident you won't run the cards back up. Cash-out refinancing converts unsecured debt into debt secured by your home — that math works great on paper, but I've watched too many borrowers clear their cards, then fill them back up within 18 months and end up with both a bigger mortgage and the credit card debt again. If the underlying spending habit isn't fixed, the refi just gives the problem more runway. When it does work, it works well: replacing 22% credit card rates with a 7% mortgage rate can save thousands per year. Just be honest with yourself about the cause first.

acceptedAnswer.text: A standard rate-and-term refinance in Austin takes 25 to 40 days from application to funding. mainEntity.name: Who qualifies for a VA loan in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: VA loan eligibility in Texas is determined by your military service record. You generally qualify if you served 90 consecutive days of active duty during wartime, 181 days during peacetime, or 6 years in the National Guard or Reserves. Veterans who were discharged under conditions other than dishonorable are eligible. Surviving spouses of service members who died in the line of duty or from a service-connected disability may also qualify. Active duty service members are eligible after 90 days of continuous service.

mainEntity.name: Do National Guard members qualify for VA loans?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. National Guard and Reserve members who have completed 6 years of service qualify for VA loan benefits. Guard and Reserve members who were activated for federal service under Title 10 orders and served 90 days of active duty may qualify even sooner. Check your DD-214 or NGB Form 22 to confirm your service dates and discharge status, then apply for your Certificate of Eligibility (COE) through VA.gov or through your lender.

mainEntity.name: What is the VA loan limit in Texas for 2026?

acceptedAnswer.text: If you have your full VA entitlement (meaning you've never used a VA loan, or you've paid off a prior VA loan and had the entitlement restored), there is no VA loan limit in Texas — you can borrow as much as a lender will approve with no down payment. The VA loan limit only applies to veterans with reduced or partial entitlement (for example, those who have an existing VA loan on another property). In those cases, the conforming loan limits set by FHFA apply to the entitlement calculation.

mainEntity.name: Can a surviving spouse use VA loan benefits?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. An unremarried surviving spouse of a veteran who died in the line of duty or from a service-connected disability is eligible to use the VA home loan benefit. Surviving spouses who remarried on or after age 57 and on or after December 16, 2003 may also be eligible. The surviving spouse applies for a Certificate of Eligibility using VA Form 26-1817 along with the veteran's discharge papers and the marriage certificate. A VA-approved lender can walk you through the documentation process.

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, the VA loan benefit is reusable. If you sell a home purchased with a VA loan and pay off the balance, your full entitlement is restored and you can use a VA loan again. If you still have an existing VA loan on a property, you can potentially use your remaining entitlement for a second VA loan — this is called a bonus or second-tier entitlement. mainEntity.name: Can I buy a new home before I sell my current one?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. The obstacle is almost never desire — it's two things: the equity for your down payment is tied up in the home you haven't sold, and the mortgage payment on your current home counts against your debt-to-income ratio when you qualify for the new one. Both have solutions. Fannie Mae will let a lender leave the current home's full housing payment out of your DTI if you provide an executed sales contract for it and confirmation that any financing contingencies have been cleared. If your current home isn't under contract yet, bridge financing or an equity-access strategy can cover the gap. The right path depends on your equity, your timing, and how much risk you want to carry.

mainEntity.name: How does my current mortgage affect qualifying for a new home?

acceptedAnswer.text: Until your current home sells, its full housing payment — principal, interest, taxes, insurance, and any HOA — counts in your debt-to-income ratio. Carrying two mortgage payments can push your DTI past program limits, which is why a lot of would-be move-up buyers think they're stuck. Fannie Mae's Selling Guide gives a path out: if your current residence is pending sale, the lender can exclude that payment from your DTI when you provide an executed sales contract and confirmation that financing contingencies have been cleared. No signed contract yet means the payment stays in your ratio unless another strategy covers it.

mainEntity.name: What is a bridge loan and when does it make sense?

acceptedAnswer.text: A bridge loan is short-term financing that lets you tap the equity in your current home to fund the down payment on your next one before the first home sells. The CFPB defines it as a temporary loan — typically 12 months or less — used to buy a new dwelling when you plan to sell the current one. It makes sense when you've identified the home you want, you have significant equity, and you need timing flexibility you don't have if you must sell first. It is not free money — it's a real loan with real costs, so it has to be weighed against the alternatives, not treated as the default.

mainEntity.name: Should I make an offer with a home-sale contingency?

acceptedAnswer.text: A home-sale contingency lets you back out if your current home doesn't sell — it protects you, but it weakens your offer, because the seller is now depending on a sale you don't control. In a competitive Austin market, a contingent offer often loses to a clean one. The strategy work is figuring out whether you actually need the contingency or whether bridge financing or an equity-access approach lets you make a stronger, non-contingent offer instead. Removing a contingency you don't need can be the difference between winning the house and watching it go to someone else.

mainEntity.name: Is buying before selling a good idea in the Austin market?

acceptedAnswer.text: It can be the right move if you have significant equity, you're relocating or moving up and need to be in the next home on a specific timeline, and you want to avoid the cost and disruption of temporary housing and a double move. It's a worse idea if your equity is thin, your income can't comfortably carry both payments for a stretch, or the bridge costs outweigh the convenience. mainEntity.name: What is a physician mortgage loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: A physician mortgage (or doctor loan) is a portfolio loan program built for doctors and dentists. It typically allows little to no down payment, waives private mortgage insurance, and lets a borrower qualify on a signed employment contract instead of paystubs. It also treats deferred or income-driven student loan payments more favorably than a standard conventional loan. It is fully underwritten under the same ability-to-repay standards as any other mortgage.

mainEntity.name: Can doctors get a mortgage before their job starts in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: Often yes. Fannie Mae's Selling Guide allows qualifying on a future employment offer when the start date is no earlier than 30 days before the note date and no later than 90 days after it, with a fully executed, non-contingent offer and additional reserves. Many Texas physician loan programs go further and let an attending or resident close on a contract that starts after move-in, which is why doctors relocating for a new position use them.

mainEntity.name: How do physician loans handle student loan debt?

acceptedAnswer.text: On a conventional loan, a deferred student loan is counted at the documented payment or 1% of the balance, and an income-driven payment can be used if it is documented and still in effect at closing. Many physician loan programs go further and use the actual income-driven repayment amount, or exclude deferred student debt entirely, which can swing your debt-to-income ratio enough to qualify when a conventional loan will not.

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually not. Most physician programs allow 0–10% down with no private mortgage insurance, even above $1 million. Conventional financing with less than 20% down requires PMI. mainEntity.name: Are physician loans only for MDs?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Most programs cover MD, DO, DDS, DMD, DPM, and often residents, fellows, and attendings. Some include nurse practitioners, physician assistants, veterinarians, and pharmacists. Eligible degrees and titles vary by lender, so the program has to be matched to your credential.

mainEntity.name: What Is a Physician Mortgage Loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: A physician mortgage — "doctor loan" — is a portfolio product. The lender keeps it on their own books instead of selling it to Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac, which means they write their own guidelines around how doctors actually earn and owe money. Three features define it: Low to no down payment, no PMI. Most programs allow 0–10% down with zero private mortgage insurance, often well past $1 million. Contract-based income. You qualify on a signed offer letter, not 30 days of paystubs you don't have yet. Student-debt-friendly DTI. The program uses your real income-driven payment — or excludes deferred student loans entirely. None of that means the loan is loose. It's still fully underwritten to the same ability-to-repay standard as any other mortgage — the lender still has to verify your income and assets with third-party records under the CFPB's ability-to-repay rule (12 CFR 1026.43). The difference is which documents count and how the debt math runs.

mainEntity.name: Who Actually Qualifies?

acceptedAnswer.text: Eligibility is about the credential, and it's broader than people think. Most programs cover MD, DO, DDS, DMD, and DPM. mainEntity.name: Can I use TSAHC assistance with an FHA loan in Texas?

mainEntity.name: What is the Mortgage Credit Certificate (MCC) and how much can it save me?

acceptedAnswer.text: An MCC is a federal tax credit — not a deduction — that lets qualifying first-time buyers claim up to 40% of their annual mortgage interest, up to $2,000 per year, directly against their federal tax liability. On a $350,000 loan, that's a $2,000 tax credit every year you live in the home. Over 10 years: $20,000 in savings. MCCs are issued through TDHCA-approved lenders and can be combined with DPA programs.

mainEntity.name: Who qualifies as a first-time home buyer in Texas for these programs?

acceptedAnswer.text: Anyone who has not owned a primary residence in the past three years qualifies as a first-time buyer under most Texas state programs. Veterans are often exempt from this requirement. Buyers purchasing in federally designated target areas may also be exempt. Don't assume you don't qualify — the definition is broader than most people expect.

mainEntity.name: Can I combine multiple first-time buyer programs in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. A common and powerful combination is TSAHC down payment assistance (grant) paired with an MCC tax credit through TDHCA. The grant covers your down payment; the MCC saves you up to $2,000 per year on federal taxes. Add seller concessions for closing costs and you can close with very little out of pocket. Your lender will tell you which combinations are allowed based on your specific loan type.

mainEntity.name: What is a warrantable condo in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: A warrantable condo is one that meets Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac guidelines — which means it qualifies for conventional financing with standard rates. Requirements include: the HOA is not involved in any active litigation, no single entity owns more than 10% of units, at least 51% of units are owner-occupied, and the HOA maintains adequate reserves. Warrantable condos are the most financing-friendly option and usually have the widest range of loan programs available.

mainEntity.name: What is a non-warrantable condo?

acceptedAnswer.text: A non-warrantable condo fails one or more Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac requirements — it might have too many investor-owned units, active HOA litigation, inadequate reserves, or be a new construction project where less than 51% of units have sold. Non-warrantable condos can still be financed, but you need a portfolio lender or non-QM lender willing to hold the loan, and rates are typically higher.

mainEntity.name: What is a condo questionnaire and why does it matter?

acceptedAnswer.text: A condo questionnaire is a form the HOA completes that provides the lender with details about the building's financials, insurance, owner-occupancy ratio, pending litigation, and special assessments. Lenders require this on every condo purchase to determine whether the project is warrantable. If the HOA refuses to complete it, or if the answers reveal a disqualifying issue, it can kill the deal — even if the borrower is otherwise fully qualified.

mainEntity.name: Can you use an FHA loan to buy a condo in Austin TX?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, but only in FHA-approved condo projects. FHA maintains a list of approved condo communities. If the specific condo development isn't on the HUD approved list, you cannot use FHA financing unless the project goes through FHA spot approval — a process that applies to a single unit in a non-approved building. Many Austin condo communities are not FHA-approved, so this is worth checking early in your search.

mainEntity.name: Are condo mortgage rates higher than single-family home rates in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: Slightly, in most cases. Fannie Mae applies a loan-level price adjustment (LLPA) to condos that adds a small cost to the rate — typically 0.25% to 0.75% depending on your loan-to-value and credit score. For warrantable condos, this is a minor difference. For non-warrantable condos, the premium is larger. VA loans are an exception — condos financed with VA loans generally do not carry the same LLPA surcharges.

mainEntity.name: What happens if the HOA has a pending lawsuit?

acceptedAnswer.text: Any active litigation involving the HOA typically makes the condo non-warrantable for conventional financing. Minor litigation (a slip-and-fall claim covered by insurance, for example) is sometimes acceptable, but HOA lawsuits involving construction defects, neighbor disputes over common areas, or financial mismanagement usually disqualify the project. If litigation is active, you'll need a portfolio or non-QM lender who accepts non-warrantable projects.

mainEntity.name: How much do I need to put down to buy a condo in Austin TX?

acceptedAnswer.text: For a warrantable condo with conventional financing, the minimum down payment is 3% (with PMI) or 5% (without PMI for some lenders). VA loans allow 0% down for eligible veterans on VA-approved condos. FHA requires 3.5% on FHA-approved projects. For non-warrantable condos, most lenders require 10-25% down since these loans are held in portfolio rather than sold to Fannie or Freddie.

mainEntity.name: What Does "Warrantable" Actually Mean?

acceptedAnswer.text: A warrantable condo is one that Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac will buy the loan on. That matters because most conventional loans get sold to one of those two entities after closing. If they won't buy it, most lenders won't make it. To be warrantable, the condo project has to meet a set of requirements: No single investor owns more than 10% of the units (10%+ triggers "concentration risk") At least 51% of units are owner-occupied (not rentals or vacant) No active litigation involving the HOA — or only minor litigation fully covered by insurance The HOA maintains adequate reserves (typically 10%+ of annual budget, though lenders vary) The project is not primarily a hotel or timeshare operation No more than 15% of units are 60+ days delinquent on HOA dues If the building checks all those boxes, you have access to standard conventional financing — 3–5% down, competitive rates, and the widest range of loan programs.

mainEntity.name: What Is a Non-Warrantable Condo?

acceptedAnswer.text: A non-warrantable condo fails one or more of those requirements. Common reasons I see in Austin: Too many investor-owned units. Popular condo developments in central Austin often have high investor concentration — buyers who purchased for short-term rental income. If investors own more than 10% of units, the project is non-warrantable. HOA litigation. Construction defect lawsuits are the big one. If the HOA is suing the builder (or anyone else) for anything significant, conventional lenders will usually pass. New construction projects. If less than 51% of units have closed on sales, the project is considered "incomplete" by Fannie Mae. You can still get financing, but it's trickier. Inadequate reserves. If the HOA's reserve fund is underfunded, lenders get nervous about deferred maintenance and future special assessments. Non-warrantable doesn't mean you can't finance it. It means you need a lender who holds the loan in their own portfolio instead of selling it to Fannie or Freddie. Rates are typically higher — 0.5% to 1.5% above comparable warrantable condos — and down payment requirements usually start at 10–25%.

mainEntity.name: What Is a Condo Questionnaire and Why Does It Matter?

acceptedAnswer.text: Here's where deals get complicated. Every condo purchase requires the HOA to complete a condo questionnaire — a document that answers the key questions a lender needs to determine warrantability. Owner-occupancy ratio, pending litigation, insurance coverage, reserve fund balance, delinquency rate on dues. All of it. The HOA doesn't always cooperate. Some charge $200–$500 to complete it. Some take weeks. Some refuse entirely. And sometimes the answers they provide disqualify the project — even when the individual unit is perfect and the buyer is fully qualified. I've had deals fall apart because of the questionnaire. Not because the buyer wasn't ready. Because the HOA had $0 in reserves, or because someone in the complex slipped in the parking lot and there was a lawsuit pending. The buyer never knew because the realtor didn't check before making the offer. Check this first. Before the offer, if you can.

mainEntity.name: What About VA Loans for Condos in Austin?

The upside: VA loans do not carry the same loan-level price adjustments (LLPAs) that conventional condo loans do. So if you're an eligible veteran buying an approved condo, you may actually get a better rate than a conventional buyer in the same building. VA also allows 0% down on approved condos. If you're a veteran or active-duty service member, this is worth knowing. See how VA loans work in Texas.

mainEntity.name: Are Condo Mortgage Rates Higher in Austin TX?

acceptedAnswer.text: Slightly, for conventional loans — yes. Fannie Mae applies a loan-level price adjustment (LLPA) to condo loans that isn't charged on single-family homes. For a borrower with a 740 credit score at 80% LTV, the condo LLPA is typically 0.75% of the loan amount — which translates to roughly a 0.125%–0.25% higher rate in most cases. For non-warrantable condos, the rate premium is larger — portfolio lenders price for the risk they're holding. Budget 0.5%–1.5% above conventional rates as a starting point.

mainEntity.name: What Should You Check Before Making an Offer on an Austin Condo?

acceptedAnswer.text: Do these before you fall in love with a unit: Look up the HOA's litigation status. Ask your realtor to request the condo questionnaire before making an offer if possible, or check public records for any active lawsuits against the HOA or developer. Find out the investor-to-owner ratio. Your realtor can request HOA documents that show the percentage of units that are rentals vs. owner-occupied. If you plan to use FHA or VA financing, search HUD's condo approval database (search "HUD condo lookup") before making an offer. It takes 30 seconds. Ask about special assessments. mainEntity.name: What Happens If the Condo Doesn't Qualify?

acceptedAnswer.text: A few paths forward: Switch lenders. Not every lender has the same guidelines. Some portfolio lenders are more flexible on occupancy ratios or reserve requirements. If one lender turns down the project, ask specifically which requirement it failed — sometimes the fix is finding the right lender, not a different property. Non-QM or portfolio loan. If the project is genuinely non-warrantable, a non-QM or portfolio lender can still finance it. Higher rate, higher down payment — but the deal can still close. Walk away. Sometimes the right answer is to find a different unit or building. A beautiful condo with a financially troubled HOA is a liability, not just a financing challenge. If the reserves are at zero and there's a lawsuit pending, that's information about the building — not just the loan.

mainEntity.name: Condo vs. Townhouse in Austin — What's the Difference for Financing?

True condos — where you own the interior space but not the land — always require the HOA review process. If you're not sure which classification a property falls under, your lender can determine it by looking at how the property is titled and whether there's a separate HOA with shared common areas. mainEntity.name: What is DSCR and how is it calculated?

acceptedAnswer.text: DSCR (Debt Service Coverage Ratio) compares a rental property's gross monthly rent to its monthly PITIA payment (Principal, Interest, Taxes, Insurance, HOA). DSCR = Gross Monthly Rent ÷ PITIA. A ratio of 1.0 means the rent covers the payment exactly.

mainEntity.name: Is a DSCR below 1.0 automatically a bad deal?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Many investor properties in competitive Texas markets come in below 1.0 on a simple rent-to-payment calculation. That does not automatically mean weak pricing or a dead file. Credit, reserves, property type, rent source, loan structure, and program fit all matter.

mainEntity.name: What is a temporary rate buydown?

acceptedAnswer.text: A temporary rate buydown is a financing arrangement where the seller deposits a lump sum at closing that subsidizes the borrower's interest rate for the first 1–3 years. The loan is originated at the full note rate; the subsidy covers the payment difference each month.

mainEntity.name: Who pays for the buydown?

acceptedAnswer.text: Typically the seller or builder pays for the buydown as a seller concession. The funds go into a custodial escrow account and are released monthly to cover the payment difference between the reduced rate and the full note rate.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between a 2/1 and a 3/2/1 buydown?

acceptedAnswer.text: A 2/1 buydown reduces the rate by 2% in year 1 and 1% in year 2, then steps to the full note rate. A 3/2/1 reduces by 3% in year 1, 2% in year 2, 1% in year 3. The 3/2/1 provides more relief upfront but requires a larger seller deposit.

mainEntity.name: Does a buydown change my long-term interest rate?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. A temporary buydown does not change your note rate, loan amount, or long-term amortization. After the buydown period ends you pay the full note rate. The loan always amortizes at the note rate; the subsidy only covers the payment difference during the reduced years.

mainEntity.name: What happens to leftover funds if I refinance or sell?

acceptedAnswer.text: If you refinance or sell before the buydown period ends, remaining escrow funds are typically applied as a principal reduction on your payoff. This makes buydowns attractive for buyers who plan to sell or refinance within a few years.

mainEntity.name: Is a seller concession the same as a buydown?

acceptedAnswer.text: A seller concession is any contribution the seller makes toward the buyer's closing costs. A buydown is one specific use of a concession. Conventional loans cap concessions at 2–9% of purchase price depending on LTV; VA and FHA have separate limits.

mainEntity.name: Is a wraparound mortgage legal in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: Owner/seller financing is legal in Texas and regulated under Chapter 5 of the Texas Property Code. WRAP mortgages require specific disclosures and must comply with SAFE Act requirements. Always work with a real estate attorney experienced in owner financing to structure the transaction correctly.

mainEntity.name: What is the 'due-on-sale' clause risk?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most conventional mortgages contain a due-on-sale clause that allows the lender to call the full loan balance due when the property is transferred. In a WRAP, the seller's existing mortgage stays in place without lender approval, which technically triggers this clause. The risk is real but lenders rarely exercise it when payments are current. An attorney can advise on structuring to minimize exposure.

mainEntity.name: What happens if the buyer stops paying?

acceptedAnswer.text: If the buyer defaults on the WRAP loan, you must continue paying your underlying mortgage to protect your credit and avoid foreclosure on your existing lien. You can then foreclose on the buyer through the owner-finance process. This is why proper legal documentation and a solid down payment are critical.

mainEntity.name: How is the WRAP interest rate set?

acceptedAnswer.text: You and the buyer negotiate the WRAP rate. It should be high enough to generate meaningful spread above your existing rate, but low enough to attract buyers who can't or won't take a conventional loan at current market rates. Rates typically range from 1-3% above your existing rate, and below current market rates for the buyer.

mainEntity.name: Does the buyer know about my existing mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — ethical and legal seller financing requires full disclosure. The buyer must understand the WRAP structure, including your existing loan balance, rate, and the due-on-sale risk. Texas Property Code requires specific disclosures in owner-finance transactions.

mainEntity.name: Is a wraparound mortgage legal in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: Owner financing is fully legal in Texas and is governed by Chapter 5 of the Texas Property Code (Sections 5.061–5.086). Texas has some of the most detailed seller-finance laws in the country, including required disclosures, balloon payment restrictions, and mandatory annual accounting statements to the buyer. You'll want a real estate attorney experienced in Texas owner financing — not a generalist — to draft the promissory note and deed of trust correctly.

mainEntity.name: What is the due-on-sale clause risk?

acceptedAnswer.text: Almost all conventional mortgages originated in the last 30 years include a due-on-sale clause — technically allowing the lender to demand full repayment when the property transfers. In a WRAP, you're keeping your mortgage in place without lender approval, which triggers this clause. The practical risk: lenders rarely enforce it when payments are current, especially on well-performing loans. But the risk is real and should be understood. Some sellers mitigate this through a land trust structure. Talk to an attorney.

mainEntity.name: What happens if the buyer stops paying me?

acceptedAnswer.text: If the buyer defaults, your existing mortgage payment is still your obligation — the bank doesn't care about your arrangement with the buyer. You must keep paying to protect your credit and avoid foreclosure. You can then foreclose on the buyer through the Texas owner-finance process. This is why a substantial down payment matters: it gives the buyer real skin in the game and gives you a financial cushion. A good attorney will also require mortgage insurance and an escrow account for taxes and insurance.

mainEntity.name: How do I find buyers for seller financing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Owner-finance buyers are everywhere right now — self-employed borrowers who can't document income the conventional way, buyers rebuilding credit, entrepreneurs, and investors. "Owner financing available" in your listing description will generate significant inquiries. You can also list on sites that specialize in owner-finance properties. Unlike traditional buyers, these buyers often close faster with fewer contingencies because they're not dependent on bank approval.

mainEntity.name: Should I use a servicer to manage payments?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. A loan servicer (such as a title company or specialized mortgage servicer) collects the buyer's payment, forwards your underlying mortgage payment, and provides annual statements — which Texas law requires. The cost is usually $25–$50/month and is worth every penny. It keeps the transaction arm's-length, creates a paper trail for both parties, and protects you if there's ever a dispute.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between a fixed-rate and adjustable-rate mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: A fixed-rate mortgage has an interest rate that never changes, so your monthly payment stays the same for the life of the loan. An adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) starts with a lower fixed rate for an initial period — typically 5, 7, or 10 years — then adjusts annually based on a market index.

mainEntity.name: When does an adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) make sense?

acceptedAnswer.text: An ARM can make sense if you plan to sell or refinance within the initial fixed period, or if you expect interest rates to drop significantly. ARMs typically offer lower starting rates than 30-year fixed loans, which can mean meaningful savings during the initial period.

mainEntity.name: Is a fixed-rate mortgage better for buying a home in Austin TX?

acceptedAnswer.text: For most Austin buyers planning to stay 7+ years, a fixed-rate mortgage offers predictability and long-term payment stability. If rates drop after you buy, you can always refinance into a lower fixed rate without the uncertainty of annual ARM adjustments.

mainEntity.name: What is a 5/1 ARM mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: A 5/1 ARM has a fixed interest rate for the first 5 years, then adjusts once per year after that based on a benchmark index (like SOFR) plus a margin set by the lender. The '5' refers to the initial fixed period in years, and the '1' indicates it adjusts annually after that.

mainEntity.name: How much lower is the rate on an ARM compared to a 30-year fixed mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Historically, 5/1 ARM starting rates run 0.5-1.0% below 30-year fixed rates. However, the spread varies based on current market conditions. When the yield curve is flat or inverted — as it has been in recent years — the advantage of an ARM can narrow significantly.

mainEntity.name: What Is a Fixed-Rate Mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: A fixed-rate mortgage is exactly what the name suggests: the interest rate stays the same for the entire life of the loan. Whether you choose a 15-year or 30-year term, your principal and interest payment will never change from the first month to the last. This is the most popular type of mortgage in the United States, and for good reason. With a fixed-rate mortgage, your monthly payment is predictable and easy to budget around. If you lock in a rate of 6.5% today, you will still be paying 6.5% in year 20, regardless of what happens in the broader economy. The only things that can change your total monthly payment over time are adjustments to property taxes and homeowners insurance, which are typically escrowed into your payment. Fixed-rate mortgages are available in a variety of terms. The 30-year fixed is the most common, offering the lowest monthly payment spread across three decades. The 15-year fixed offers a lower interest rate and builds equity much faster, but comes with a higher monthly payment. Some lenders also offer 20-year and 25-year terms that split the difference.

mainEntity.name: What Is an Adjustable-Rate Mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: An adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) starts with a fixed interest rate for an initial period, after which the rate adjusts periodically based on a market index. The most common ARM structures are the 5/1 ARM, 7/1 ARM, and 10/1 ARM. The first number represents how many years the initial fixed rate lasts, and the second number indicates how often the rate adjusts after that. For example, a 7/1 ARM gives you a fixed rate for the first seven years. After that initial period, the rate adjusts once per year based on a benchmark index (such as the Secured Overnight Financing Rate, or SOFR) plus a margin set by the lender. If the index goes up, your rate goes up. If it goes down, your rate goes down. ARMs include built-in protections called rate caps that limit how much the rate can change. There are typically three caps: an initial adjustment cap (how much the rate can change at the first adjustment), a periodic cap (how much it can change at each subsequent adjustment), and a lifetime cap (the maximum the rate can ever reach over the life of the loan). A common cap structure is 2/2/5, meaning the rate cannot increase more than 2% at the first adjustment, 2% at each subsequent adjustment, and 5% total over the life of the loan. The key advantage of an ARM is that the initial fixed rate is usually lower than what you would get on a comparable fixed-rate mortgage. This lower starting rate means a lower monthly payment during the initial period.

mainEntity.name: When Does Each Make Sense?

acceptedAnswer.text: A fixed-rate mortgage makes the most sense when: You plan to stay in the home for more than 7 to 10 years. You value the certainty of a predictable payment and want to budget with confidence. Current interest rates are historically low and you want to lock in that rate for the long term. You are risk-averse and do not want to worry about potential rate increases in the future. An adjustable-rate mortgage makes the most sense when: You plan to sell or refinance before the initial fixed period ends. If you know you will move within five to seven years, a 5/1 or 7/1 ARM lets you take advantage of the lower rate without facing the adjustment period. Interest rates are currently high and widely expected to decrease. An ARM allows you to benefit from falling rates without refinancing. You want to maximize your purchasing power. The lower initial rate on an ARM may allow you to qualify for a higher loan amount or afford a larger payment toward principal. You expect your income to increase significantly in the coming years, making potential future payment increases manageable.

mainEntity.name: What Is a Mortgage Broker?

acceptedAnswer.text: A mortgage broker is a licensed professional who acts as a middleman between you and multiple lenders. Instead of offering only one company's loan products, a broker shops your loan across a network of wholesale lenders to compare rate, cost, and program tradeoffs for your specific situation. Think of it like the difference between buying insurance directly from one company versus working with an independent insurance agent who compares quotes from a dozen carriers. The broker does not lend their own money. They originate the loan, handle the paperwork, and coordinate the process, but the funding comes from the wholesale lender they match you with. Mortgage brokers are licensed and regulated by the NMLS (Nationwide Multistate Licensing System) and must meet continuing education requirements in every state where they operate.

mainEntity.name: What Is a Bank or Direct Lender?

acceptedAnswer.text: A bank or direct lender funds your mortgage with their own money (or money they have borrowed). When you walk into Chase, Wells Fargo, or a local credit union and apply for a mortgage, you are working with a direct lender. They offer their own loan products at their own rates, and their loan officers can only sell you what that one institution offers. Some direct lenders also include large online companies like Rocket Mortgage or Better.com. These are not banks in the traditional sense, but they function the same way: they offer only their own products at their own pricing.

mainEntity.name: Do Mortgage Brokers Get Lower Rates Than Banks?

acceptedAnswer.text: This is usually the biggest question: who gets me the better rate? A mortgage broker has access to wholesale rates from multiple lenders. These wholesale rates are often lower than the retail rates a bank offers directly to consumers, because wholesale lenders do not have to cover the overhead costs of branch locations, marketing, and large sales teams. The broker earns their compensation separately, and the total cost to the borrower is frequently lower than what a single bank offers. A bank offers one set of rates: theirs. If their pricing is not competitive on the day you lock, you have no recourse other than to start over with a different lender. With a broker, if one lender's pricing moves unfavorably, the broker can pivot to another lender without starting your application over from scratch. The bottom line: brokers can usually match or beat bank rates because they are comparing pricing across multiple lenders in real time.

mainEntity.name: Do Mortgage Brokers Have More Loan Options Than Banks?

acceptedAnswer.text: Banks are limited to their own menu of loan products. If your situation does not fit neatly into their guidelines, you may be declined or pushed into a product that is not ideal for you. Some banks have strong conventional loan programs but weak FHA or VA options, or vice versa. A broker has access to dozens of lenders, each with their own set of guidelines and loan products. If one lender cannot accommodate your situation, the broker can often find another one that can, without making you start a new application. This flexibility is especially valuable for borrowers with non-traditional income (self-employed, 1099, commission-based), lower credit scores, or unique property types. For example, I regularly work with borrowers who were turned down by a bank but qualified with one of my capital partners that has more flexible guidelines for the same loan type. mainEntity.name: How Does Service and Communication Compare Between a Broker and a Bank?

acceptedAnswer.text: At a large bank, your loan may be processed by a team you never meet. You might work with one person during the application, another during underwriting, and a third at closing. Turnover at big lenders is high, and your loan is one of hundreds being processed simultaneously. With a mortgage broker, you typically work directly with the broker (or a small team) throughout the entire process. You have a direct line to someone who knows your file inside and out. When an issue comes up, you get a call from a person who actually understands your situation, not a generic status update from an automated system. This is one of the reasons my clients and realtor partners consistently mention communication as the thing that sets our process apart. When you call or text, you get a real answer from someone who knows your deal.

mainEntity.name: Can a Mortgage Broker Close Faster Than a Bank?

acceptedAnswer.text: Big banks are not known for fast closings. Their volume is enormous, their processes are rigid, and delays are common. It is not unusual for a bank loan to take 45 to 60 days to close. Brokers working with nimble wholesale lenders can often close faster. Many of our transactions close in a timeline driven by program, property, appraisal, and documentation, and we have closed in as few as 14 days when needed. Speed matters in a competitive market like Austin, where sellers may favor offers with shorter closing timelines.

mainEntity.name: Should You Use a Mortgage Broker or a Bank?

acceptedAnswer.text: I will not pretend to be unbiased here. I am a mortgage broker because I genuinely believe it is a better model for most borrowers. Shopping multiple lenders, offering competitive wholesale rates, providing hands-on personal service, and closing faster is a combination that is hard for any single bank to match. That said, the most important thing is working with someone you trust, someone who explains your options clearly, communicates throughout the process, and delivers on their commitments. Whether that person works at a bank or a brokerage, find someone who does the job well. If you want to see what a broker can do for you, reach out anytime. I am happy to run the numbers, compare options, and let the results speak for themselves.

mainEntity.name: Why did mortgage rates go up in 2026?

acceptedAnswer.text: Mortgage rates rose in 2026 because of an energy-driven inflation shock. Conflict in the Middle East sent oil prices surging, which pushed up gasoline, transportation, and energy costs across the economy. When inflation rises, bond investors demand higher returns on long-term bonds, and mortgage rates follow those bond yields. As a result, rates that briefly dipped below 6% earlier in the year climbed back into the mid-6% range.

mainEntity.name: How does the Iran peace deal affect mortgage rates?

acceptedAnswer.text: The U.S.-Iran peace agreement could reopen important oil shipping routes and restore global oil supplies. Oil prices dropped sharply after the announcement, and lower energy costs can ease inflation over time, which is supportive of lower mortgage rates. But the effect is gradual, not immediate. It will likely take months for global oil production and shipping to fully normalize, so the impact on inflation and rates will be slow rather than overnight.

mainEntity.name: Will mortgage rates drop below 6% in 2026?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is unlikely in the near future. Inflation remains above the Federal Reserve's target, so the market is no longer expecting aggressive rate cuts anytime soon. The most likely path is mortgage rates staying in the mid-6% range for much of 2026, with gradual improvement as inflation cools, rather than a return to the 2-3% rates seen during COVID.

mainEntity.name: Do mortgage rates follow the Federal Reserve?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not directly. Many people assume mortgage rates simply follow whatever the Fed does, but rates are influenced more by inflation expectations and the bond market than by the Fed's short-term rate decisions. The Fed shapes the broader environment, but it is long-term bond yields, driven by inflation, that move mortgage rates day to day.

mainEntity.name: Should I wait for lower rates before buying a home?

acceptedAnswer.text: Waiting carries its own cost. While buyers wait for rates to fall, home prices, rents, and competition often keep rising. If you are holding out for 5% rates before making a move, you may be waiting longer than expected. Today's buyers also have more leverage than a few years ago, including more inventory, seller concessions, and rate buydowns. Remember, you can refinance a rate later, but you cannot go back and buy the home you missed.

mainEntity.name: What is the mortgage rate forecast for the rest of 2026?

acceptedAnswer.text: No one can predict rates with certainty, but the most likely scenario is rates holding in the mid-6% range for much of 2026, with gradual improvement as inflation continues to cool. Expect periods of volatility tied to energy prices and global events. The outlook improves if oil prices keep falling, inflation readings improve over the coming months, global tensions stay contained, and growth slows enough to ease inflation without causing a recession.

mainEntity.name: What questions should I ask a mortgage lender before committing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Five questions that matter: (1) Are you a broker or a direct lender — and how many rate options can you show me? (2) What's your average close time, and have you closed loans in tight timelines when the file supports it? (3) Will you be my point of contact through closing, or does my file get handed off? (4) What's your availability — can I reach you on nights and weekends when I'm writing offers? (5) How do your rates compare to what I've seen advertised — and can you break down the closing costs line by line? Any lender worth working with will answer these without hesitation.

mainEntity.name: Should I just go with the lender my realtor recommends?

acceptedAnswer.text: Realtor referrals are a good starting point — realtors refer lenders they've seen perform under pressure, which matters in Austin's competitive market. But it's not a reason to skip your own research. Get a quote from the referred lender and at least one mortgage broker. Compare the Loan Estimate side by side — same loan amount, same term, same rate — and look at the APR and total closing costs, not just the rate. A referral gets you a candidate. You make the hire.

mainEntity.name: Is the lowest rate always the best deal?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Rate is one line item. A 0.125% lower rate on a $400,000 loan saves about $30/month — but if the closing costs are $2,000 higher to get that rate, you've paid extra to break even in five years. Compare the APR (annual percentage rate), which folds in fees, not just the note rate. Also factor in service quality: a lender who misses your closing date costs you far more than any rate difference. In Austin's market, deals fall apart when lenders don't perform — choose someone with a proven track record.

mainEntity.name: How do I compare lenders fairly?

Compare Section A (origination fees), Section B (third-party fees), and the APR on page 3. If a lender won't give you a Loan Estimate or quotes verbally only, that's a red flag.

mainEntity.name: What's the difference between APR and interest rate?

acceptedAnswer.text: Your interest rate is the percentage the lender charges on your loan balance — it determines your monthly payment. APR (annual percentage rate) takes that rate and adds in lender fees like origination charges, discount points, and certain closing costs, then spreads them across the full loan term. APR is always higher than or equal to your interest rate. The gap between the two tells you how much the lender's fees add to your annual cost.

mainEntity.name: Is a lower APR always better?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. APR assumes you keep the loan for its full 30-year term. If you sell or refinance in 5–7 years — which most people do — a loan with higher APR but lower upfront fees can cost less overall. The only way to know which loan actually saves you money is to calculate the total cost over the time you plan to keep it: monthly payment times months, plus all closing costs.

mainEntity.name: Should I choose the mortgage with the lowest APR?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not automatically. APR is one data point, not the whole picture. If two loans have identical terms and you plan to keep the loan for 20+ years, the lower APR is usually the better deal. But if you expect to move or refinance within 5–10 years, calculate total cost over your actual holding period instead. Take (monthly payment times number of months) plus total closing costs for each option. That gives you a real apples-to-apples comparison.

mainEntity.name: Can I negotiate my mortgage origination fee?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. The origination fee is the lender's profit margin on your loan and is fully negotiable. It appears in Section A of your Loan Estimate. Some lenders charge 1% of the loan amount, others charge a flat fee, and some build it into the rate instead. If you have a competing Loan Estimate showing lower origination charges, most lenders will consider matching or reducing their fee to keep your business.

mainEntity.name: What mortgage closing costs are negotiable?

acceptedAnswer.text: Lender-controlled fees are negotiable: origination charges, discount points, rate lock fees, and application fees. These all appear in Section A of your Loan Estimate. Third-party fees — appraisal, title insurance, recording fees, property taxes, and prepaid interest — are generally not negotiable because they are set by outside parties, not the lender. You can sometimes shop for your own title company or attorney to reduce those costs, but the lender does not control them.

mainEntity.name: How do I get a lender to lower their fees?

acceptedAnswer.text: The most effective approach is to get a Loan Estimate from a second lender and show it to the first. Lenders know when you are comparing, and most would rather reduce their margin than lose the deal entirely. Focus your comparison on Section A (origination charges) since those are the fees the lender controls. If a lender will not explain their pricing or refuses to discuss it, that tells you something about how that relationship will go through closing.

mainEntity.name: What is Section A on a Loan Estimate?

This is the only section on page 2 that varies significantly between lenders. Sections B through H cover third-party costs like appraisals, title insurance, and government recording fees — those are roughly the same regardless of which lender you choose.

acceptedAnswer.text: Not always. Online lenders advertise rates that assume an 780+ credit score, 20% down, and owner-occupied primary residence. Always compare using the full Loan Estimate, not just the advertised rate.

A correspondent lender — what I am — funds loans in my own name, controls the file end to end, and usually beats both on pricing for Austin and Central Texas buyers.

mainEntity.name: Are online mortgage rates really lower?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not always. Online lenders advertise rates that assume an 780+ credit score, 20% down, and an owner-occupied primary residence. Once Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac loan-level price adjustments are applied for your actual credit, down payment, and property type, your rate can move 0.25%–0.75% off the advertised number. The fees on your Loan Estimate — origination charges, discount points, underwriting fees — can also erase any rate advantage. Always compare using the full Loan Estimate, not just the advertised rate.

mainEntity.name: What's a correspondent lender, and why does it matter?

acceptedAnswer.text: A correspondent lender funds loans in its own name using its own warehouse line of credit, then sells the closed loan to investors. That's different from a broker, who submits files to a wholesale lender that funds in their name. For borrowers, the correspondent model usually means faster closings, more control over conditions and pricing, and competitive wholesale-style rates without the retail markup of a big bank or online lender. I'm a correspondent lender licensed in Texas and can also broker deals when wholesale pricing makes more sense for the specific loan.

mainEntity.name: Should I wait for mortgage rates to drop before buying a home?

acceptedAnswer.text: Waiting for rates to drop usually costs more than it saves. Every month you wait, you pay rent instead of building equity. When rates do drop, buyer demand surges and home prices rise — often offsetting the rate savings entirely. The better question is whether you're financially ready to buy today.

mainEntity.name: What happens to home prices when mortgage rates drop?

acceptedAnswer.text: When rates drop, purchasing power increases across the buyer pool, which drives up demand and typically pushes home prices higher — sometimes quickly. Buyers who waited for the rate drop end up competing against more buyers for the same homes, often at higher prices. The rate savings can be partially or fully erased by a higher purchase price.

mainEntity.name: Can I refinance my mortgage later if rates drop after I buy?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. This is the 'marry the house, date the rate' strategy. You buy now at current rates and refinance when rates improve. Refinancing typically costs 1-3% of the loan amount and breaks even within 18-36 months. You get to lock in today's home price while still benefiting from future rate drops.

mainEntity.name: How do Austin TX buyers decide when to buy a home?

acceptedAnswer.text: The best time to buy depends more on personal readiness than on market conditions. If you have stable income, adequate savings for down payment and reserves, a solid credit profile, and plan to stay at least 3-5 years, the math typically favors buying sooner rather than waiting for perfect rates.

mainEntity.name: What is the 'date the rate, marry the house' strategy?

acceptedAnswer.text: This means focusing on finding the right home at today's price, accepting current interest rates, and planning to refinance when rates eventually fall. The strategy eliminates the risk of being priced out of the market while waiting for rate improvement — and lets you start building equity immediately.

mainEntity.name: Should You Wait for Rates to Drop Before You Sell and Buy?

acceptedAnswer.text: March 4, 2026 · 4 min read I get this question constantly. And I get it — the math feels obvious. Wait for rates to drop, then sell, then buy. Lock in the lower rate on the new house. Makes sense on paper. Here's the problem: everyone else is thinking the exact same thing. When rates drop — and they will eventually — the buyers who've been sitting on the sidelines all flood the market at once. Inventory gets eaten up fast. Multiple offers come back. Home prices spike. That rate savings you were waiting for? It can disappear inside 60 days once demand surges. The math most people miss: A 1% drop in rates saves you roughly $150/month on a $400K loan. But if home prices rise 5% while you were waiting, you just added $20,000 to your purchase price. You never catch up. So what's the right framework? Here's how I walk my clients through it. Question 1: Do you actually need to move? If the answer is yes — growing family, job change, life event — then timing the market is the wrong conversation. You make the move work financially, and you do it on your schedule, not the Fed's. If it's a "want to" move, then waiting has less downside and more flexibility. Either way, know which conversation you're in. Question 2: What's your current rate, and what would you be buying at? If you're sitting on a 3% rate from 2021, that's a real cost to move — you're trading a low-rate asset. That math matters. We should run it together before you make any decisions. If your current rate is already in the 6–7% range, the pain of moving is much lower. You're not sacrificing much, and you might find a home worth buying before prices climb. Question 3: Can you buy first and refinance later? This is the part most people overlook. Today's rate isn't your rate forever. Buy the right house now, at today's price, in today's market. Then refinance when rates come down. You get the house you want. You get the lower rate when it arrives. You don't have to compete against a wave of new buyers in a hot market. The phrase I use with clients: "Date the rate. Marry the house." The rate is temporary. The purchase price is permanent. None of this is a blanket answer. Every situation is different — your equity, your target price range, your timeline, your financial cushion. That's exactly what I'm here to help you think through. If you've been sitting on this question, let's just run the numbers. It costs nothing to look, and it usually answers the question faster than you'd expect.

mainEntity.name: What credit score do I need to qualify for a mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Minimum scores vary by loan type: 620 for conventional loans, 580 for FHA with 3.5% down (or 500 with 10% down), and 620 for VA loans. A higher score unlocks better rates — even a 20-point improvement can save thousands in interest over the life of the loan.

mainEntity.name: How long does it take to improve my credit score enough to get a mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Paying down credit card balances can improve your score within 30-60 days. Disputing errors on your credit report can also show quick improvement. More serious issues like collections, charge-offs, or late payments typically take 6-24 months to recover from, depending on severity.

mainEntity.name: Does getting a mortgage pre-approval hurt my credit score?

acceptedAnswer.text: A pre-approval requires a hard credit inquiry, which typically lowers your score by 2-5 points temporarily. Multiple mortgage inquiries within a 14-45 day window are treated as a single inquiry by the credit bureaus, so shopping multiple lenders during that period won't cause additional damage.

mainEntity.name: What factors affect my credit score most for mortgage approval?

acceptedAnswer.text: Payment history is the biggest factor at 35% of your score — every on-time payment helps, every late payment hurts. Credit utilization (how much of your available credit you're using) accounts for 30%. Length of credit history is 15%, while new credit accounts and credit mix each contribute 10%.

mainEntity.name: Should I pay off collections before applying for a mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on the loan type and the collection balance. Some loan programs allow collections to remain unpaid if they are older or below a certain threshold. However, paying or settling collections can improve your score — and removing them via a pay-for-delete agreement is even better. Consult your loan officer before paying off old collections, as it can sometimes trigger a temporary score drop.

mainEntity.name: What is DTI in a mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: DTI (Debt-to-Income ratio) is the percentage of your gross monthly income that goes toward monthly debt payments. Lenders use two DTI numbers: front-end DTI (housing payment only) and back-end DTI (all debts including housing, car loans, student loans, and credit cards). Most conventional loans require a back-end DTI below 45%, though some programs allow up to 50%. A lower DTI means you qualify for more loan programs and better rates.

mainEntity.name: What is LTV in a mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: LTV (Loan-to-Value ratio) is the percentage of the home's value covered by your mortgage. If you buy a $400,000 home with $80,000 down (20%), your LTV is 80%. LTV determines whether you need PMI, what rate you qualify for, and which loan programs are available. Lower LTV means less risk for the lender and typically a lower rate for the borrower.

mainEntity.name: What is PMI and when do I have to pay it?

acceptedAnswer.text: PMI (Private Mortgage Insurance) is required on conventional loans when your down payment is less than 20% — meaning your LTV is above 80%. PMI protects the lender (not you) if you default. PMI rates typically run 0.3%–1.5% of the loan amount per year. PMI automatically cancels when your LTV reaches 78% of the original purchase price. You can also request removal when you reach 80% LTV based on current market value by paying for a new appraisal.

mainEntity.name: What is a mortgage rate lock?

acceptedAnswer.text: A rate lock is a lender's guarantee to hold a specific interest rate and points for a defined period — typically 15 to 60 days — while your loan processes. If rates rise before closing, your locked rate stays the same. If rates fall, your locked rate stays the same (unless you negotiate a float-down option). Lock periods expire: missing your closing date means re-locking, often at a higher cost.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between pre-qualification and pre-approval?

acceptedAnswer.text: Pre-qualification is an informal estimate of what you might borrow based on self-reported income and assets — no credit check, no document review. Pre-approval is a formal lender review: your credit is pulled, income and assets are verified, and the lender issues a written commitment for a specific loan amount. In Austin's competitive market, sellers typically require a pre-approval letter, not just a pre-qualification, before accepting an offer.

mainEntity.name: What does Clear to Close (CTC) mean?

acceptedAnswer.text: Clear to Close (CTC) means the underwriter has reviewed and approved all loan conditions — your file is fully approved and ready to fund. After CTC, you'll receive your final Closing Disclosure at least three business days before closing (required by TRID). CTC is the finish line of the mortgage process before you sign and get your keys.
